evidence.quote: An alternate route going around the south, west, and north shores of the lake can be accessed from Route 45.

evidence.claim: Shore roads circle a lake whose outlet powered New Preston’s mills
evidence.quote: numerous mills and modestly scaled factories were constructed along the East Aspetuck River, which drops precipitously between its source at Lake Waramaug and the New Preston village center, providing a robust source of water power.

evidence.claim: Lake Waramaug’s shore roads pass houses, seasonal cottages and boathouses, with Route 45 along the eastern shore and unsigned Special Service Road 478 looping along the other three sides.
evidence.quote: The shoreline development of Lake Waramaug is moderate and includes houses, seasonal cottages, and boat houses, with few commercial establishments.

evidence.claim: In New Preston, the surrounding terrain has steep hills, narrow valleys and exposed ledge rock.
evidence.quote: The terrain is characterized by steep hills and narrow valleys, with a preponderance of talus slopes and ledge rock.

evidence.claim: Connecticut’s Department of Transportation designated the lake’s perimeter roads as state scenic roads in 1996, with protection against changes that would diminish their scenic qualities.
evidence.quote: In 1996, the Connecticut Department of Transportation designated the 6.9 miles (11.1 km) of perimeter roads around Lake Waramaug as state scenic roads, affording them a legal status that discourages maintenance or improvements that would detract from the roads' scenic qualities.

evidence.claim: The New Preston road north through Warren became state Highway 152 in 1922, then Route 45 in the 1932 renumbering.
evidence.quote: The road from New Preston to Warren center, and continuing north up to the Housatonic River south of Cornwall Bridge, was designated as a state highway in 1922. It was then known as Highway 152. Old Highway 152 was renumbered to Route 45 as part of the 1932 state highway renumbering.

evidence.claim: Scenic designation extended through New Preston village in 2010, along with the US 202 section between Route 45 and Rabbit Hill Road.
evidence.quote: In 2010, New Preston's main commercial thoroughfare, East Shore Road (also known as Connecticut Route 45), was designated a state scenic road, together with a 2.8-mile (4.5 km) portion of Route 202 extending northeast from the junction with Route 45 to Rabbit Hill Road.

evidence.claim: Start in Marbledale on US 202 and continue to New Preston, where the East Aspetuck River carries the lake’s outflow over New Preston Falls.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 202 runs east–west in the northern part of town, connecting the villages of Marbledale, New Preston, and Woodville.

evidence.claim: Route 45 leads north along the east shore into Warren.
evidence.quote: It heads north along the eastern shore of Lake Waramaug and soon enters the town of  Warren.

evidence.claim: North Shore Road leads west toward Lake Waramaug State Park on the northwest shore.
evidence.quote: The park can be reached by taking Route 45 north from Route 202 and turning west onto North Shore Road.

evidence.claim: The unsigned loop continues along the west and south shores to Route 45.
evidence.quote: An alternate route going around the south, west, and north shores of the lake can be accessed from Route 45. This western loop is an unsigned state highway known as Special Service Road 478.

evidence.claim: Route 45 along the eastern shore and unsigned Special Service Road 478 looping along the other three sides.
evidence.quote: It heads north along the eastern shore of Lake Waramaug and soon enters the town of  Warren. In Warren, the road is known as Lake Road. An alternate route going around the south, west, and north shores of the lake can be accessed from Route 45. This western loop is an unsigned state highway known as Special Service Road 478.

evidence.claim: the East Aspetuck River carries the lake’s outflow over New Preston Falls.
evidence.quote: the headwaters of the East Aspetuck River, which runs through the village center and over New Preston Falls.

evidence.claim: Lake Waramaug State Park on the northwest shore.
evidence.quote: located on the northwest shore of Lake Waramaug

evidence.claim: St. Andrew’s gives Marbledale a distinctive roadside detail: Gothic lancet windows with marble sills set into a brick church.
evidence.quote: It has Gothic-style lancet windows with marble sills and wood frames.

evidence.claim: Its square tower projects from the building, with wood finishing the upper stages.
evidence.quote: It is a brick structure with a projecting square tower whose upper stages are finished in wood

evidence.claim: The congregation began in New Preston in 1764, abandoned its original building during Revolutionary War harassment, and later used a former Quaker meeting house.
evidence.quote: The St. Andrew's Episcopalian congregation was established in 1764 in New Preston. The largely Loyalist congregation was harassed during the American Revolutionary War, and abandoned its original building, meeting in private homes.

evidence.claim: The present church belongs to the early 1820s and was enlarged in 1855.
evidence.quote: The present edifice was begun in 1821 and completed in 1823. The church was enlarged in 1855

evidence.claim: It stands on New Milford Turnpike at Wheaton Road.
evidence.quote: St. Andrew's is located on the south side of New Milford Turnpike at its junction with Wheaton Road.

evidence.claim: later used a former Quaker meeting house.
evidence.quote: Formed anew in 1791, the congregation rented and then purchased a local Quaker meeting house

evidence.claim: The church’s lancet windows have marble sills and wood frames.
evidence.quote: It has Gothic-style lancet windows with marble sills and wood frames.

evidence.claim: The East Aspetuck drops sharply from Lake Waramaug into New Preston, where it runs through the village center and over the falls.
evidence.quote: the headwaters of the East Aspetuck River, which runs through the village center and over New Preston Falls.

evidence.claim: That descent powered mills and small factories in the early nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: In the early decades of the 19th century (the era of the Industrial Revolution), numerous mills and modestly scaled factories were constructed along the East Aspetuck River, which drops precipitously between its source at Lake Waramaug and the New Preston village center, providing a robust source of water power.

evidence.claim: Manufacturers made twine, hats, cheese boxes, ax handles, shoes and harnesses.
evidence.quote: New Preston housed an iron works, as well as manufacturers of twine, hats, cheese boxes, ax handles, shoes, and harnesses.

evidence.claim: Industry later declined as electricity, expanding rail networks and larger manufacturing centers changed production.
evidence.quote: with the advent of electricity, expansion of national rail networks, and the rise of larger, more accessible manufacturing centers during the latter part of the 19th century, industrial activity in New Preston decreased

evidence.claim: Several nineteenth-century mill structures remain along the river, among the village’s collection of Georgian, Greek Revival, Italianate and Shingle-style homes.
evidence.quote: many well-preserved 18th and 19th century homes built in the Georgian, Greek Revival, Italianate, and Shingle styles, as well as several 19th-century mill structures along the East Aspetuck River.

evidence.claim: The East Aspetuck River runs through the village center and over New Preston Falls.
evidence.quote: the East Aspetuck River, which runs through the village center and over New Preston Falls.

evidence.claim: Connecticut bought the first 75 acres of Lake Waramaug State Park in 1920.
evidence.quote: The state park's first 75 acres (30 ha) were purchased by the state in 1920.

evidence.claim: The park occupies the lake’s northwest shore in Kent and covers 95 acres.
evidence.quote: Lake Waramaug State Park is a 95-acre (38 ha) public recreation area located on the northwest shore of Lake Waramaug in the town of Kent

evidence.claim: Beyond it, the lake’s developed shoreline includes houses, seasonal cottages and boathouses.
evidence.quote: The shoreline development of Lake Waramaug is moderate and includes houses, seasonal cottages, and boat houses

evidence.claim: The water itself is natural in origin, though a small concrete and masonry dam has raised its surface.
evidence.quote: Although natural in origin, the surface elevation of the lake has been raised by a small concrete and masonry dam.

evidence.claim: Sucker Brook, smaller streams and groundwater feed the lake; its outflow runs south into the East Aspetuck River.
evidence.quote: The lake is fed by Sucker Brook (Lake Waramaug Brook), numerous small streams, and groundwater that enters through the lake bottom. Drainage from Waramaug Lake flows southward into the East Aspetuck River.

evidence.claim: The shoreline’s summer houses followed another transport change: the Shepaug Railroad arrived in 1872, bringing passenger service from New York City and prompting construction of homes and inns beside the lake. Rail operations ended in 1948.
evidence.quote: With the arrival of the Shepaug Railroad in 1872, passenger service was introduced between New Preston Station and New York City, which gave rise to the construction of summer homes and inns around the perimeter of Lake Waramaug.

evidence.claim: Rail operations ended in 1948.
evidence.quote: The railroad ceased operation in 1948

evidence.claim: During the nineteenth century, the village supported a prosperous cooper’s shop. Marbledale is one of five villages within the town of Washington.
evidence.quote: During the 19th century, Marbledale was the site of a prosperous cooper's shop.

evidence.claim: Marbledale is one of five villages within the town of Washington.
evidence.quote: Marbledale is one of five villages in the rural town of Washington.

evidence.claim: The steep, rocky terrain limited building sites, and most viable sites were already in use before 1900, leaving little room for new construction.
evidence.quote: Because New Preston's steep, rocky terrain presents significant constraints to development, most viable development sites were utilized prior to 1900, making contemporary construction of new homes and businesses rare.

evidence.claim: The lake reaches a maximum depth of 40 feet. Its steep underwater slopes hold gravel, cobbles and boulders, while flatter bottom areas contain sand, mud and organic muck.
evidence.quote: The lake has a maximum depth of 40 feet (12 m)

evidence.claim: Its steep underwater slopes hold gravel, cobbles and boulders, while flatter bottom areas contain sand, mud and organic muck.
evidence.quote: The bottom materials on steep side slopes of the lake consist primarily of gravel, cobbles, and boulders, whereas the flatter areas consist primarily of sand, mud, and organic muck.

flags: Only Wikipedia pages are cached. Scenic designation is documented, but no designating-body statement explaining its selection is available; no evaluative rationale is invented.
Route 45’s stated 0.6-mile scenic length conflicts with its mileposts; New Preston and US 202 pages give 2.8 versus 3.8 miles for the same designated US 202 section. Lengths are omitted.
The current claim that the state park is the only public access conflicts with the lake page’s nonresident town-launch arrangement. Omitted, along with unsupported driving pace (slow loop).
St. Andrew’s is dated 1822 in summaries but construction is dated 1821–1823 in the detailed history. Use early 1820s.
Park recreation logistics are omitted without a cached manager source. River is retained as the closest permitted scene value for the lake; no lake scene is allowed.
